title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used the hosted model gpt‑5‑mini under adapter enforcement of shared‑initial generation and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present the sealed design, deterministic reconciliation, representative examples from archived artifacts, contamination‑check evidence (10% Mininet holdout → 20 tasks; zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative LLMs promises operational productivity but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages or violate policies. Architectures that combine LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate→validate→repair, GVR) aim to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. The operational benefit of automated repair depends on the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures, validator coverage/fidelity, and repair budget/effectiveness. We therefore asked a narrowly scoped confirmatory question (preregistered): Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Contributions: (1) a sealed preregistered paired design (n = 200) enforcing shared‑initial generation to isolate validator+repair effects on the same candidate; (2) a fully archived autonomous execution with deterministic reconciliation and complete accounting (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0); (3) an honest, artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome and interpretation clarifying when automated repair can and cannot reduce validator‑detected failures, plus reproducibility notes and operational recommendations grounded in archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: Prior work documents LLM factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism, and proposes mitigation approaches including grounding (RAG), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded/guarded agent architectures. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration synthesis but often lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate studies or external validation. Architectural proposals integrate LLMs with deterministic network validators (e.g., Batfish‑style checkers) and repair loops to improve safety; red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies show tool‑description injection and tool‑chaining can change safety outcomes materially. Surveys and prototype evaluations motivate externally auditable, preregistered measurements that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model and prompt policy. Our study positions itself among these generator→validator→repair proposals by measuring the preregistered paired estimand under tightly controlled, archived conditions using a deterministic validator and an independent emulator holdout for contamination checks.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration. The study preregistration (cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02) specified a paired design with n = 200 tasks (4 topology clusters × 50 tasks), shared_initial generation semantics (one deterministic initial candidate per task reused across conditions), a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), and a preplanned primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided (α = 0.05) on paired binary outcomes (validator pass/fail). The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; 95% CIs used a bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈ 30% and targeted a 50% relative reduction; the preregistration froze stopping rules (max model calls = 400: 200 initial + up to 200 repair calls), inclusion/exclusion rules, contamination plan, and missingness handling prior to any model calls.

Task bank, validators, and contamination control. We used a curated machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks spanning enterprise, campus, datacenter, and edge topologies. Each task encodes initial and expected final states, explicit workflow constraints (for example: make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields), and required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces task‑encoded constraints and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the contamination summary artifact records zero disagreements. The preregistration and contamination plan deterministically exclude tasks with validator–emulator disagreement from primary analysis and prespecify sensitivity analyses for alternative treatments.

Generation semantics, adapter enforcement, and repair policy. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation: for each task the system performed one deterministic initial model invocation (adapter accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}), and the same generated candidate was used for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. The registered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM per task if the primary validator reported violations; up to 200 repair calls were therefore permitted but only if initial candidates failed validation. Missingness and exclusion rules were applied deterministically per the preregistration.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair_calls_used = 0 because no initial candidate failed the primary validator. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts report all consistency checks passed (pair_accounting_consistent = true, episode_accounting_consistent = true). Provider accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, cache_hit_count = 0, confirming single generator invocations per task reused across conditions.

Primary inferential outcome. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. With no discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is not testable because there were no baseline validator failures to reduce.

Representative artifacts and diagnostics. Representative per‑task artifacts (e.g., pair‑000001 .. pair‑000006) show shared initial generator outputs that matched the required_sequence and passed validation: validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0 in each record. Example pair‑000001 normalized_response: "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up" which matches the stored reference_answer and validator normalized_configuration. Difficulty annotations (make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) and parsed_command_count/required_command_count in validator traces confirm tasks exercised medium‑to‑very_hard workflow constraints despite the validator‑passing outputs.

Contamination and holdout. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed; analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero validator–emulator disagreements. We disclose a reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed for the Mininet holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the bundle, which prevents deterministic reconstruction of which specific tasks constituted the holdout despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate confirmatory outcome illustrates a logical boundary condition: when the chosen model, prompt policy, and adapter produce validator‑passing candidates for all items in a workload, an automatic validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This is a substantive operational datum: measured marginal value of repair is conditional on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage.

Why baseline failures were zero (artifact‑grounded). The archived evidence supports several nonexclusive factors: (1) the prompt template and shared_initial semantics produced candidates that directly satisfied the explicit task‑bank constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes clear required_sequences that map directly to deterministic validator checks and so are easier for a deterministic, low‑temperature generation policy to satisfy; (3) the primary validator enforces these task‑encoded constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor‑specific behaviors visible only under end‑to‑end execution; and (4) the single repair budget combined with shared_initial enforcement removes per‑condition re‑sampling as a route to generate alternative, repairable candidates.

Operational implications. Before investing in automated repair, operators should measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative production workloads and inspect validator coverage via end‑to‑end emulation. Where baseline validator failures are rare, resources often yield higher return when spent improving validator fidelity ( richer device semantics, vendor idiosyncrasies), adversarial testing, multi‑sample/multi‑model generation, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals. Conversely, when baseline failures are nontrivial, a GVR architecture with an adequate repair budget and well‑engineered repair prompts can reduce validator‑detected issues; realized gains depend on validator completeness and repair effectiveness.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: preregistration, adapter enforcement, and deterministic accounting reduce post‑hoc bias, but shared_initial design intentionally sacrifices per‑condition sampling variance to isolate marginal repair effects. Construct validity: the primary validator verifies task‑encoded constraints but can miss real device idiosyncrasies or emergent runtime failures visible only under full device emulation or on real hardware. External validity: single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), single sampling policy (shared initial), curated synthetic/public task bank, and single repair budget limit transferability; different models, temperatures, multi‑sample generation, or adversarial distributions may yield different baseline failure prevalences. Conclusion validity: the McNemar test is uninformative for zero discordant pairs; nevertheless reporting the observed zero‑discordance is a meaningful operational observation that should inform future workload selection and power planning.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), so the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated on this task bank. The result demonstrates that the marginal operational value of automated repair is workload dependent: when baseline validator failures are rare, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future work should (artifact‑grounded) evaluate GVR on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, extend validator fidelity with richer emulator/real‑device checks, examine multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for independent inspection.

Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
